title: 1.2 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can make sense of a problem, plan a strategy, and use fractions of a whole number to compare quantities, explain how I can tell, and judge a case I have not seen before.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

noticeAndWonder.context: Three students set off walking along different paths through the same neighborhood. Each one takes a different route, and none of them has finished yet.
noticeStarters: I notice the three paths are ___ .
wonderStarters: I wonder how far each student ___ .
I wonder how we could figure out ___ .

vocabulary.definition: An amount in a problem — a number with a meaning attached, like 540 meters.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una cantidad en un problema: un número con un significado, como 540 metros.
vocabulary.example: The heights of the buildings are the quantities in the problem.

vocabulary.definition: How two quantities compare or connect to each other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cómo se comparan o se conectan dos cantidades entre sí.
vocabulary.example: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel.

vocabulary.definition: A plan for how to solve a problem before you start computing.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un plan para resolver un problema antes de empezar a calcular.
vocabulary.example: We can think about how the quantities in the problem relate.

vocabulary.definition: A solution that makes sense in the context of the problem.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una solución que tiene sentido en el contexto del problema.
vocabulary.example: A building that is 5/6 of 540 meters must be less than 540 meters.

vocabulary.definition: To keep working on a problem, checking your progress and adjusting your plan when you get stuck.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Seguir trabajando en un problema, revisando tu progreso y ajustando tu plan cuando te atascas.
vocabulary.example: When you hit a dead end, you try another strategy instead of quitting.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 1.2. You can already get the answer — so in here the answer is the starting point. We ask when the method holds, when it breaks, and how you would convince someone who disagrees.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — Make sense, plan, check
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. So we go up a level, not up a number: find what is always true, show it a second way, and be ready to defend it with a reason instead of an answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: When we do math, we make sense of problems, develop a solution plan, check our progress, and try other strategies when we come to dead ends — and you can say why it is true, and where it would stop being true.

iDo.title: Watch me estimate the peas
lines: I do not count every pea — I look for a group I CAN count, like one small cluster of about 10.
Then I ask how many of those clusters would cover the whole picture.
If about 12 clusters fit, my estimate is about 120 peas — a reasoned answer, close enough to be useful.

explore.label: Comparing Walks: sort what the problem tells you.
categories: We KNOW this from the problem

cards.text: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel
Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel
The exact number of miles Deon walked

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Analyzing a problem starts with separating what you know from what you don't. After sorting, tell a partner: can you still figure out who walked the SHORTEST distance, even without any exact numbers? As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

connect.scenario: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, and Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel. You never learn the exact distances — but the relationships still tell you a lot.
connect.promptQuestion: How can you use the relationships among the distances to choose possible values for how far Deon, Miguel, and Evelyn walked?
connect.prompt: Pick a distance for Miguel. Then choose a distance for Deon that is ___ than Miguel's and a distance for Evelyn that is ___ than Miguel's, and explain how you ___ that your three values work.

check.stem: In the Comparing Walks problem, Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, and Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel. Without any exact distances, what can you determine?
choices: The order from shortest to longest: Deon, Miguel, Evelyn
Nothing — you need exact numbers before you can compare
Deon and Evelyn walked the same distance
Evelyn walked the shortest distance
check.explanation: The two relationships alone place all three students in order — Deon below Miguel, Evelyn above Miguel — with no exact numbers needed; Evelyn walked LONGER than Miguel, not shorter.

check.stem: A student picks Miguel = 2 miles, Deon = 2.5 miles, Evelyn = 1.5 miles. What is wrong with these values?
choices: Deon's distance is greater than Miguel's, which breaks “shorter than”
Nothing is wrong — any three distances work
Evelyn's distance is too small compared to Deon's
Miguel's distance must always be the smallest of the three
check.explanation: Deon must walk LESS than Miguel, but 2.5 > 2 — the student swapped Deon's and Evelyn's values, which is exactly the check the Connect task asks you to run.

check.stem: Building height problem: which statement shows you are CHECKING your solution against the relationship in the problem?
choices: “5/6 is less than 1, so my answer for London should be less than 540 meters”
“My answer is 650 meters, and that seems like a big number so it's probably right”
“I don't need to check once I've multiplied”
“Since I used a fraction, the answer must be exact”
check.explanation: Checking means comparing your answer's reasonableness against the relationship in the problem — a fraction less than 1 must give a result less than 540 — not just judging whether a number looks big or trusting the operation alone.

connect.modelAnswer: I let Miguel walk 2 miles. Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, so I chose 1.5 miles for Deon. Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel, so I chose 2.5 miles for Evelyn. I checked both relationships: 1.5 < 2 and 2.5 > 2, so my values fit. Any values work as long as Deon's is less than Miguel's and Evelyn's is greater.

onLevel.stem: The Rio de Janeiro building will be 9/10 as tall as One World Trade Center (540 meters). How tall will it be?
choices: 486 meters
54 meters
4,860 meters
594 meters
onLevel.explanation: 9/10 × 540: one tenth of 540 is 54, and 9 tenths is 9 × 54 = 486 meters.
choiceFeedback: 54 meters is only 1/10 of 540 — you still need 9 of those tenths.
4,860 meters multiplies 540 by 9 but never divides by 10.
594 meters ADDS one tenth (540 + 54) instead of taking 9 tenths of 540.
hints: First find one tenth of 540.
Multiply that tenth by 9.

onLevel.stem: The Tokyo building will be 6/5 as tall as One World Trade Center (540 meters). How tall will it be?
choices: 648 meters
450 meters
108 meters
432 meters
onLevel.explanation: 6/5 × 540: one fifth of 540 is 108, and 6 fifths is 6 × 108 = 648 meters — taller than 540, because 6/5 is greater than 1.
choiceFeedback: 450 meters is 5/6 of 540 — that flips the fraction, and it belongs to the London building.
108 meters is only 1/5 of 540 — you still need 6 of those fifths.
432 meters SUBTRACTS a fifth (540 − 108) instead of taking 6 fifths.
hints: First find one fifth of 540.
6/5 means six of those fifths — will that be more or less than 540?

onLevel.stem: Without calculating, which new building must be TALLER than One World Trade Center, and why?
choices: Tokyo, because 6/5 is greater than 1
London, because 5/6 has a 6 in it
Rio de Janeiro, because 9/10 is close to 1
None — a fraction of 540 is always less than 540
onLevel.explanation: Multiplying 540 by a fraction greater than 1 gives more than 540. Only 6/5 is greater than 1; 5/6 and 9/10 are both less than 1.
choiceFeedback: The 6 in 5/6 is the denominator — 5/6 is less than 1, so the London building is SHORTER than 540 meters.
Close to 1 is not greater than 1 — 9/10 of 540 is still less than 540 meters.
A fraction GREATER than 1, like 6/5, makes the product greater than 540.
hints: Compare each fraction to 1.
Multiplying by a fraction greater than 1 makes the result bigger.

onLevel.stem: Suppose Miguel walked 2 miles. Choose possible distances for Deon and Evelyn that fit the problem, and explain how you checked them.
onLevel.modelAnswer: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, so Deon could have walked 1.5 miles. Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel, so Evelyn could have walked 2.5 miles. I checked: 1.5 < 2 and 2.5 > 2, so both relationships are true.

extending.stem: You calculate 5/6 × 540 and get 650 meters. What does the checking step of your plan tell you?
choices: The answer is unreasonable — 5/6 of 540 must be LESS than 540
The answer is fine because it is close to 540
The answer is fine because 650 is a bigger number than 5/6
Checking is only needed when the problem asks for it
extending.explanation: 5/6 is less than 1, so 5/6 of 540 must land below 540. Getting 650 means the plan needs adjusting — which is exactly what checking is for.
choiceFeedback: Close to 540 is not the test — the answer must be BELOW 540, because 5/6 is less than 1.
Comparing 650 to the fraction 5/6 mixes up two different kinds of quantities — compare the answer to 540 instead.
This lesson says we check our progress on EVERY problem, not only when asked.
hints: Is 5/6 more or less than 1?
Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes the result smaller.
So should the answer be above or below 540?

extending.stem: The lesson says we check on our progress toward a solution and adjust our plan as needed. Describe one way YOU can check on your progress while solving a problem.
extending.modelAnswer: I can stop partway and ask whether my numbers still make sense in the story — for example, if a building is supposed to be a fraction less than 1 of 540 meters, my answer so far should be under 540. If it isn't, I go back and adjust my plan.
sentenceStems: One way I check my progress is ___ .
If something doesn't make sense, I ___ .

extending.stem: Which set shows FIVE different correct decompositions of 105.76?
extending.explanation: All five in the first set rebuild 105.76 exactly — by addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
choiceFeedback: 105 + 7.6 = 112.6, so that set contains an error.
52.88 × 3 = 158.64, so that set contains an error.
hints: Check every member of each set.
One wrong member spoils the whole set.
Find the set where all five land exactly on 105.76.

extending.stem: Without computing the exact heights, order the three new buildings from shortest to tallest. (London: 5/6 of 540 m, Rio de Janeiro: 9/10 of 540 m, Tokyo: 6/5 of 540 m.)
choices: London, Rio de Janeiro, Tokyo
Rio de Janeiro, London, Tokyo
Tokyo, Rio de Janeiro, London
London, Tokyo, Rio de Janeiro
extending.explanation: Compare the fractions: 5/6 ≈ 0.83 is less than 9/10 = 0.9, and both are less than 6/5 = 1.2. Same whole, so the order of the fractions is the order of the heights.
choiceFeedback: That puts 9/10 below 5/6 — but 9/10 = 0.9 is GREATER than 5/6 ≈ 0.83.
That is tallest to shortest — the question asks for shortest to tallest.
Tokyo's 6/5 is greater than 1, so Tokyo must be last, not in the middle.
hints: All three are fractions of the SAME 540 meters, so just compare the fractions.
Compare each fraction to 1, then compare 5/6 and 9/10 to each other.

extending.stem: A classmate says, "In math, only the final answer matters." Using this lesson, write what you would say back.
extending.modelAnswer: I would say the thinking matters just as much. In the buildings problem we knew London and Rio would be under 540 meters and Tokyo would be over BEFORE calculating, because we compared the fractions to 1. That checking is what catches mistakes — when we do math, we make sense of problems, check our progress, and try other strategies at dead ends.
sentenceStems: One example from this lesson is ___ .

extending.stem: Write your own Comparing Walks problem: describe three people using only relationships (shorter than, longer than), so a reader can put them in order without any exact distances. Then give one set of values that fits.
extending.modelAnswer: Ava ran a shorter distance than Ben, and Cora ran a longer distance than Ben. The order must be Ava, then Ben, then Cora. One set of values that fits: Ava 3 km, Ben 4 km, Cora 5.5 km, because 3 < 4 and 5.5 > 4.
sentenceStems: ___ walked a shorter distance than ___ , and ___ walked a longer distance than ___ .
One set of values that fits is ___ because ___ .

extending.stem: Which of these is a correct way to decompose 105.76?
extending.explanation: 100 + 5.76 = 105.76. Decomposing means the parts must rebuild the original number exactly.
choiceFeedback: 100 + 5.076 = 105.076 — that pushes the digits one decimal place too far right.
105 + 7.6 = 112.6, not 105.76 — the 7 and 6 belong in the tenths and hundredths places.
10 + 5.76 = 15.76 — that drops the hundreds digit of 105.76.
hints: Add each option and compare to 105.76.
The parts must total 105.76 exactly.

extending.stem: Which is another correct decomposition of 105.76?
extending.explanation: 110 − 4.24 = 105.76. A decomposition can use subtraction, not only addition.
choiceFeedback: 110 − 5.24 = 104.76 — that takes away one whole too many.
106 − 0.34 = 105.66 — the difference from 106 is 0.24, not 0.34.
110 + 4.24 = 114.24 — that moves away from 105.76 instead of down to it.
hints: Start at 110. How far down is 105.76?
So subtracting 4.24 from 110 works.

practice.commonMistake: Expecting a fraction of a number to be bigger than the number — 5/6 × 540 must be LESS than 540 because 5/6 is less than 1; only a fraction greater than 1, like 6/5, makes the product bigger.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — Which statement best shows what this lesson means by "math is exploring and thinking"?
choices: We make sense of problems, plan a strategy, check our progress, and try other strategies at dead ends
We compute as fast as possible and move on to the next problem
We wait for someone to show us the one correct method
We only check our work when the answer looks wrong
exitTicket.explanation: The summary names the whole cycle: make sense of the problem, develop a plan, check progress and adjust, and make sense of the solution in context.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It describes a cycle, not a single step.
Which option includes making sense, planning, AND checking?

turnAndTalk.question: The book decomposes 105.76 as one example: 100 + 5.76. Why must the parts of a decomposition always rebuild the original number exactly?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The lesson's warm-up decomposes 105.76 several different ways, and each decomposition must sum back to 105.76.
turnAndTalk.extend: Find a decomposition of 105.76 that is different from 100 + 5.76, and prove it also sums to 105.76.
extendStems: My decomposition is ___ + ___, and it equals ___.
I checked it was correct by ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You sorted 'Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel' as something we KNOW, even without exact numbers. How can a relationship like 'shorter than' be knowledge, if we don't know the actual distance?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The Comparing Walks problem tells us Deon walked less than Miguel and Evelyn walked more than Miguel, without giving any exact distances.

stems.en: We know this because the problem states a ___, not an exact number.
stems.es: Sabemos esto porque el problema da una ___, no un número exacto.

turnAndTalk.extend: Can you determine who walked the SHORTEST distance among all three students using only the relationships given? Justify your order.
extendStems: The order from shortest to longest is ___, ___, ___ because ___.
I can be sure of this order even without numbers because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: If you pick a distance for Miguel, how do you choose distances for Deon and Evelyn that stay true to the relationships in the problem?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Deon's distance must be shorter than Miguel's, and Evelyn's distance must be longer than Miguel's — any values that satisfy both relationships work.

stems.en: I picked ___ miles for Miguel, so Deon must be ___ and Evelyn must be ___.
stems.es: Elegí ___ millas para Miguel, así que Deon debe ser ___ y Evelyn debe ser ___.

stems.en: I checked my values worked by ___.
stems.es: Comprobé que mis valores funcionaban al ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: Could two different students pick completely different sets of three distances and BOTH be correct? Explain why or why not.
extendStems: Yes/No, because the relationships only require ___.
Another valid set of distances could be ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on decomposing numbers, what strategy did you use when a decomposition felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Decomposing a number like 105.76 means breaking it into parts that must add back to the original, place value by place value.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who wrote 100 + 5.076 for 105.76? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ because ___.
Their mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

Use the visual model, then complete one step at a time.
